quote: That damn John didn’t come to the party.
note: (6a). *Damn* is an attributive modifier in the subject NP. Other prenominal tokens: (6b), (8b), (11a), (14) on p. 10, (49) "You damn fool!" on p. 44. She calls it "the expressive adjective damn" (p. 7).

quote: In these examples, it is clear that the content of the nominal appositives is not affected by the negation or by the conditional, and similarly for the expressive adjective damn.
note: Verdict on (6a), p. 6. Host relation: integrated (inside the subject of the negated clause).

quote: In these examples, it is clear that the content of the nominal appositives is not affected by the negation or by the conditional, and similarly for the expressive adjective damn.
note: Covers the conditional (6b), "If that damn John comes to the party, no one will have a good time." (p. 6), which P11N doesn't cover.

quote: In these sentences, the content of the appositive, that John is a swimmer, and of the expressive adjective, that John is in some way bad, is indeed projected.
note: The content is stated as evaluative.

quote: # If I hate John, then that damn John came to the party.
note: (8b), marked #. The previous row's quotation is her verdict: the content projects and isn't bound by the antecedent.

quote: A: That damn John came to the party last night.
note: (11). B replies "That’s not true/That’s false." This bears on P07 only indirectly: she never says *damn* adds nothing at-issue. P07 comes through class row C1.

quote: ≠ ‘There’s nothing wrong with John.’
note: (11). B replies "That’s not true/That’s false." This bears on P07 only indirectly: she never says *damn* adds nothing at-issue. P07 comes through class row C1.

quote: the degree of difficulty seems to be different for the cases of green and (e.g.) damn. A paraphrase of the latter cannot even be attempted without using expressives
note: Footnote 13. The use isn't specified (bare lexeme), but all her *damn* examples are prenominal. Answers Geurts's *green* objection (§3).

quote: by the content of ‘(I) hate the damn/fucking Germans.’
note: Example (14): "If I hate the {damn, fucking} Germans, then he is a Kraut." I changed the brace separator from a pipe to avoid breaking the table. This is her only mention of *fucking* (Geurts 2007's title aside). *Damn* and *fucking* are material in "an expressive paraphrase" (p. 9) of Kraut's content. No property of *fucking* itself is stated. Also supports DAMN_PRENOM P03.

quote: (38a) is an appropriate utterance in either Situation 1 or Situation 2.
note: (38a) "Ouch!" (toe stub / poke in the eye). Also (35c) "Ouch!" on p. 34, classed as a fully expressive exclamation (C11–C15).

quote: But the main point for our purposes here is that ouch is a bearer of purely expressive content.
note: See also C11. Caveat in footnote 46 (§3).

quote: If we assume that ouch denotes something of type t s , though, we can avoid this situation.
note: t^s. The argument: other particles modify *ouch*, and t^c content can't be an operator's input.

quote: These considerations are enough to make it clear that man is in fact doing something to the meaning of ouch in (38b), and so some kind of composition is at work.
note: (36) "Ouch, man!" / "Man, ouch!" works in both orders (p. 35). (38b) "Ouch, man!" "gives an impression of blame" (p. 35). This is a claim about semantic composition, not about syntactic dependency.

quote: It turns out that these modifiers can also modify purely expressive items in some dialects of English.
note: (40) "Totally ouch(, dude)." Restricted to some dialects. The modifiers are the McCready & Schwager intensifiers (*totally*, *fully*).

quote: Thanks!
note: (35a), given under "Another kind of even more obvious case is that of expressives that do not perform any modification" (p. 34), "such as salutations or fully expressive exclama-tions" (hyphenated across the line). Its other properties come only through C11–C15.

quote: (= Bill is not very rich.)
note: Incidental. (48) "Bill, the philanthropist, is very rich." with the reply "That’s not true." Her point is about the appositive, and she says nothing about *very*. The gloss puts *very*'s contribution in deniable at-issue content.

quote: CIE items, by definition, do not participate in at-issue semantic processes
note: Members illustrated: nominal appositives, *damn*, pejoratives ((12): negation, *might*, question). Footnote 7 calls this "the Potts generalizations about scope independence and denial". The first clause also bears on P07 at class level.

quote: In particular, they are not affected by semantic operators.
note: Members illustrated: nominal appositives, *damn*, pejoratives ((12): negation, *might*, question). Footnote 7 calls this "the Potts generalizations about scope independence and denial". The first clause also bears on P07 at class level.

quote: CIE content does not participate in denials.
note: Members: appositive (10), *damn* (11), Kraut (15). Narrowed on p. 41 to truth-directed denials (§3).

quote: Such binding does not happen for CIE content.
note: Separates CIE content from presupposition: "In this respect, CIE content is similar to presupposition. It differs in that it cannot be bound" (p. 7). Members: (8a), (8b) *damn*, Kraut (13)–(14).

quote: according to which expressives have the property of ‘ineffability,’ meaning that they literally cannot be paraphrased in ways not involving other expressives
note: She endorses it: "I think Potts is right in distinguishing the two types" (footnote 13). Named member: *damn*.

quote: the function of (emotive) expressives is to narrow down a subinterval of R used as a model of a range of emotion displayed with respect to some object
note: Footnote 15. She says she won't use this system. No members named.

quote: supplementary CI content, which always seems to show non-resource-sensitive behavior
note: Also p. 14: "This difference can be taken as a significant generalization about supplementary CI(E)s." Members: nominal appositives and "(some) speaker-oriented adverbials" (p. 14), e.g. "Frankly speaking" (1b, p. 2). She never assigns prenominal *damn* a type, so don't infer that it's supplementary.

quote: types for those semantic objects that ‘shunt’ information from one dimension to another, without leaving anything behind
note: These are resource-sensitive CIE types. Assigned to: the CIE side of every mixed item; stand-alone *man*; Ouch!; Thanks! and Good morning. (t^c or t^s); *man* and *totally* as ⟨t^s,t^s⟩ operators (p. 36); *yokumo*; Quechua *-si*; *daroo*. Tentatively also exclamatives (p. 43) and "You damn fool!" (p. 44).

quote: First, it should introduce content in both at-issue and CIE dimensions.
note: Page 5 adds: "Introducing content in both dimensions is the essential criterion." English members: pejoratives (Kraut, Boche, Frog, Yankee; Jap may be decomposable), epithets (*bum*, *asshole*), colored terms (*steed*, *nag*). Non-English members: Japanese honorific verbs, benefactive *morau*, tu/vous and tu/usted, Viennese *ur*, Quechua *-chá*. None of the 46 bearers.

quote: The second criterion is that it should be monomorphemic.
note: Page 5 adds: "Introducing content in both dimensions is the essential criterion." English members: pejoratives (Kraut, Boche, Frog, Yankee; Jap may be decomposable), epithets (*bum*, *asshole*), colored terms (*steed*, *nag*). Non-English members: Japanese honorific verbs, benefactive *morau*, tu/vous and tu/usted, Viennese *ur*, Quechua *-chá*. None of the 46 bearers.

quote: they can serve as main predicates and are affected (in part) by various semantic operators
note: Assigns at-issue content. Compare "Here, ‘Kraut’ obviously must contribute to at-issue content" (p. 6).

quote: giving a multimorphemic analysis to epithets like bum or asshole
note: The uses don't match ours. These are argument-NP uses (footnote 33, p. 23, Japanese *kojiki* glossed "That bum did too"), not BASTARD_SUPP's supplement or YOU_BASTARD's exclamatory NP, and *bastard* isn't named. Classing them as mixed entails at-issue content, so P07 is N for this class by the schema's negative standard. She doesn't say what that at-issue content is.

quote: it seems much more natural just to analyze them as mixed content bearers
note: The uses don't match ours. These are argument-NP uses (footnote 33, p. 23, Japanese *kojiki* glossed "That bum did too"), not BASTARD_SUPP's supplement or YOU_BASTARD's exclamatory NP, and *bastard* isn't named. Classing them as mixed entails at-issue content, so P07 is N for this class by the schema's negative standard. She doesn't say what that at-issue content is.

item_id: C11 CLASS:non-modifying expressives (salutations, fully expressive exclamations)
quote: Expressions like these lack truth conditions, though they can be expressively correct (appropriate) or not. They plainly do not assert anything
note: Said of (35a) Thanks!, (35b) Good morning., (35c) Ouch!, plus *man* on its second analysis. HELLO isn't named; *Good morning* is her salutation. Caveat in footnote 46 (§3).

quote: Expressions like these lack truth conditions, though they can be expressively correct (appropriate) or not. They plainly do not assert anything
note: Introduced on p. 32: "one can think of a notion of ‘expressive correctness,’ following Kaplan".

quote: in cases like these, the expressive (or conventionally implicated) content is the main content of the utterance
where the content is not functional and expresses a constant
note: Contrasts with functional main CIEs (*man* modifying a proposition, *yokumo*). She first allows t^c or t^s, then rejects t^c because other particles modify these items.

quote: which is one way to view purely expressive single-expression utterances
note: Points forward to §3. It frames these as a type of utterance, so it isn't just a bare solitary token.

quote: Clearly, on either analysis, stand-alone particles provide another case where the conventionally implicated content is the primary content of the utterance.
note: Only *man* is named (not one of the 46); LAH isn't mentioned.

quote: But certain operators are able to act on expressive particles such as those discussed by Kaplan: namely, other particles.
note: *Ouch* is modified and *man* is the modifier.

quote: Utterances like this one do not exhibit any at-issue content; there is nothing for truth-directed denials to target, for example.
note: (49) "You damn fool!", after Potts & Roeper (2006). YOU_BASTARD is the same construction, but *bastard* isn't named. The *damn* inside it is DAMN_PRENOM.

quote: This fact makes it look like shunting types should be involved.
note: Hedged. She adds that she cannot improve on Potts & Roeper.

quote: expressive small clauses, sentential phrases like (49), discussed by Potts & Roeper (2006).
note: (49) is treated as a whole utterance ("Utterances like this one").

quote: bears the usual hallmarks of emotive expressive meanings: for example, it is highly context dependent with respect to positivity and negativity
note: Said of Viennese *ur*. Footnote 50 (p. 38) extends it to *yokumo* and *man*: "These facts are reminiscent of what we find with modification by the particle man". No bearer named.

item_id: C22 CLASS:expressive content (Potts et al. 2009, reported)
quote: These authors argue that expressive content does not participate in a number of grammatical operations that intuitively involve identity, such as anaphora.
note: Footnote 33. The illustration is Japanese only.

quote: exclamatives, which have the combinatory properties one would expect from shunting-typed objects in terms of further combinatorics
note: Hedged ("given certain assumptions"). This is a clause type, and no bearer is named.
